summary:
Terra Analog Mission Control is an explainable Earth–Mars terrain comparison tool that turns NASA open data into testable exploration questions. It compares a defined 20 km Gale Crater/Aeolis Palus reference window with five curated Earth candidate windows using median slope, terrain roughness, and relative relief from MOLA and NASADEM data.

Rather than presenting a black-box “best site,” the platform shows each candidate’s similarity score, raw terrain values, feature contributions, source datasets, operational hypothesis, and limitations. This helps students, science communicators, and future exploration researchers understand both why a terrain comparison is useful and where it breaks down.

The project is important because terrestrial analogs can support rover-traversal, instrument, and geology questions before field validation. Terra Analog Mission Control makes this process transparent, reproducible, and scientifically bounded: it generates candidate hypotheses, not landing-site recommendations or proven analogs.

details:
Terra Analog Mission Control

What it does

Terra Analog Mission Control is an explainable Earth–Mars terrain comparison platform. It compares a defined 20 km reference window in Gale Crater / Aeolis Palus with five curated Earth candidate windows.

The MVP uses three reproducible terrain features:

  • Median slope
  • Terrain roughness
  • Relative relief

Each candidate receives a similarity score from 0–100, but the score is never shown as a verdict. Users can inspect the raw terrain values, feature contributions, source dataset IDs, data coverage, operational hypothesis, and candidate-specific limitations.

How it works

  1. We derive comparable terrain features from Mars MOLA MEGDR and Earth NASADEM HGT V001 data.
  2. We analyze both bodies at a declared 500 m analysis resolution with a 3 km local window.
    • Slope: 0.35
    • Roughness: 0.35
    • Relative relief: 0.30
  3. The web app only shows production results when every score has complete provenance, feature contributions, and caveats.

Benefits and intended impact

The project helps students, science communicators, and future exploration researchers turn open planetary data into testable Earth-based questions. It can support early discussions around rover traversal, instrument testing, terrain navigation, and geological-process study.

Its intended impact is to make planetary comparison more accessible without hiding scientific uncertainty. Rather than implying that Earth can replicate Mars, it makes differences visible and encourages field validation and expert review.

Technology used

  • Next.js, TypeScript, React, and Tailwind CSS
  • Supabase PostgreSQL and Row Level Security
  • Python-based offline terrain-feature and ranking pipeline
  • Zod validation for API and provenance contracts
  • NASA PDS MOLA MEGDR and NASA EOSDIS NASADEM datasets
  • Git-based reproducibility, checksums, automated validation tests, and scientific-claim guardrails

What makes it creative

Terra Analog Mission Control makes the breakdown of an analogy as important as the match. Instead of hiding uncertainty behind an “AI discovery” claim, it shows why a candidate ranked highly, which features differ, which datasets were used, and what remains unmodeled.

Scientific considerations

We explicitly considered different sensor resolutions, vertical reference systems, scaling across Earth and Mars, data completeness, provenance, and reproducibility. The MVP does not model gravity, atmosphere, radiation, temperature regimes, biological activity, access, safety, regulation, or land permissions. Therefore, it produces candidate hypotheses for further study, not proven analogs, rover-safety assessments, or mission-site recommendations.
